title: Computer ethics and unethical practices
definition:
Computer ethics are the moral principles that guide us to use computers, software, and the Internet in a responsible, legal, and respectful way. They are the rules of good behaviour in the digital world, helping us decide what is right and what is wrong when we work with technology. Just as we follow traffic rules on the roads and classroom rules in school, we need computer ethics to keep the online world safe and fair for everyone. These principles become especially important when we remember that the same computer or the same Internet connection can be used to help people or to harm them.

In the previous node you have already studied that the Internet is a powerful double-edged tool. It gives us instant communication through email, chat, video calls, and social media, and it puts a vast amount of information at our fingertips. On the other hand, it can also lead to addiction, expose users to inappropriate content, and create privacy risks. Because the Internet can be used for both good and bad purposes, computer ethics provide the boundaries that encourage good use and reduce the bad use. They turn the Internet from a risky place into a useful and trustworthy one.

Three major unethical practices that break these moral rules are plagiarism, software piracy, and hacking. Plagiarism is the act of taking another person's work, ideas, words, images, or program code and presenting them as your own without giving credit to the original creator. It is unethical because it is a form of stealing that takes away recognition from the real author and misleads the person who reads or checks the work. Software piracy is the unauthorised copying, distribution, or use of software, games, music, movies, or any other digital product without the permission of the owner or without paying for it. It is harmful because it breaks the law and causes financial loss to the creators who invested time and money in making the product. Hacking is the unauthorised access to a computer, network, account, or system. It is dangerous because it violates privacy, can steal personal or secret information, and may damage important systems. We must not confuse this with ethical hacking, which is done by trained professionals with permission to test and improve security, just like a security guard testing locks.

Following computer ethics means being a responsible digital citizen. It means using the Internet for information and communication, respecting other people's work and privacy, giving proper credit whenever we use someone else's ideas, and using only legally obtained software. It also means understanding that our actions online can affect real people and real society. When we practise these principles, we protect ourselves and others from the disadvantages of the Internet, such as cybercrime, loss of privacy, and loss of trust.
textWalkthrough:
Think back to the last big idea you met in Class 6, when you studied machine language, assembly language, and high-level languages. Those lessons taught you that computers are incredibly powerful machines, but they only do what people instruct them to do through programs. Now you are ready for the next step: learning the rules that should guide the people who give those instructions and use the results. In this node you move from the question, "How do I make a computer work?" to the question, "How do I use a computer responsibly?" That is the leap from the depth prerequisite C6_CS_002 to the ethics you are studying today.

Before we go further, also look back at the direct prerequisite C7_CS_010, where you saw the Internet as a double-sided tool. On the helpful side, it gives instant communication and access to information. On the risky side, it can lead to addiction, inappropriate content, and privacy risks. Can you see why the topic of ethics follows naturally? Once you know that the Internet can be used to help or to harm, you need a set of moral rules—computer ethics—to encourage the helpful use and to prevent the harmful use. The unethical practices you are about to study are exactly the kinds of behaviour that turn the Internet's advantages into disadvantages.

Let us start with the central question: What are computer ethics? Imagine you are in a school computer lab in a city like Bengaluru, Pune, or Chennai. You have a computer in front of you with access to the whole world. Computer ethics are the invisible rules that tell you to be honest, careful, and respectful while using that machine. They include not damaging the hardware, not disturbing other students, and—not to be forgotten—not harming people through the files and messages you create or share.

Now consider the first unethical practice, plagiarism. A good answer would say, "Plagiarism is claiming another person's work, ideas, words, or program code as your own without giving credit or citation." A weak answer would simply say, "Plagiarism is copying." Why is the second version weak? Because it does not show that you understand the idea of credit. When you copy a paragraph from a website and paste it into your project without saying where it came from, you are taking credit for someone else's effort. A strong student always acknowledges the original author by giving credit.

Next, think about software piracy. A strong answer explains that software piracy is the unauthorised copying, distribution, or use of software. It is not only about downloading free movies; it is about using any program without paying for it or without the owner's permission. Imagine a small Indian software company in Hyderabad that spends months creating a useful educational app for school students. If people copy that app illegally, the company loses money and may stop making good products. That is why piracy is harmful to individuals, businesses, and society.

Then there is hacking. Many students get confused here, so let us be clear. Hacking, in the ordinary and harmful sense, is the unauthorised access to computer systems, accounts, or networks. It is like entering someone's house without permission. A good answer distinguishes this from ethical hacking, which is done with permission to test and improve security—just like a security guard checking the locks of a bank. When you mention ethical hacking in the exam, make sure you include the words "with permission."

Remember, this node is only about understanding the rules and the three main unethical practices. You do not need to learn cyber laws or intellectual property rights in detail here, because those are reserved for later classes. You should, however, quickly revise the good computing habits you learned earlier about caring for hardware and software, since they are also part of responsible behaviour.

In the ICSE and ISC board exams, examiners expect clear and complete definitions, not vague one-liners. CISCE examiner observations have repeatedly shown that common errors occur when students do not review the fundamentals. So when you answer, use the exact words from the vocabulary—computer ethics, responsible, unethical, plagiarism, piracy, hacking, ethical hacking, and credit—and give a short, Indian example to show that you truly understand.

In the Indian context, this could mean installing a paid operating system or an app without a licence. It is illegal and harmful because it takes income away from the creators and can spread unsafe, modified files.
diagnosticText:
Q1 (recall): Define computer ethics and list the three unethical practices mentioned in the syllabus.
Answer: Computer ethics are the moral principles that guide people to use computers, software, and the Internet in a responsible, legal, and respectful way. They help us understand the right way to behave online and protect both ourselves and others. The three main unethical practices are plagiarism, software piracy, and hacking. Plagiarism is claiming another person's work or ideas as your own without giving credit. Software piracy is the unauthorised copying, distribution, or use of software without the owner's permission. Hacking is the unauthorised access to a computer system, network, or account. Each of these practices is harmful because it breaks the trust and safety that make the digital world useful.

Q2 (reasoning): Why is plagiarism considered unethical? Explain how it is different from using someone else's work and giving them credit.
Answer: Plagiarism is unethical because it is a form of dishonesty and intellectual stealing. When a student takes someone else's words, ideas, pictures, or program code and presents them as if they were their own, they are taking credit for work they did not do. This is unfair to the original author, who spent time and effort to create the work. It also misleads the teacher, examiner, or reader, who believes the work belongs to the student. The result is a loss of trust and a loss of learning, because the student did not practise the skill themselves. Using someone else's work with credit is completely different. In that case, the student clearly says who the original author is, perhaps by writing the author's name in brackets or in a list of sources. This is honest and respectful. It shows that the student has read and understood the work, and it allows the reader to find the original. Giving credit turns borrowing into learning, while plagiarism turns borrowing into stealing.

Q3 (evaluate): "A student argues that hacking is not wrong if the hacker is very skilled and no one gets hurt." Evaluate this statement.
Answer: This statement is mostly incorrect, and the reason is the missing word: permission. Hacking, when it means unauthorised access to a computer system or network, is wrong even if the person is very skilled and even if no visible harm is done. The act itself is a violation of privacy and safety, just like entering someone's locked house without permission is wrong, even if nothing is stolen. The computer system belongs to someone, and the owner has the right to control who enters. When a skilled person enters a system without that owner's permission, they break the law and break the trust that the owner and users had in the system's safety. The argument about skill is also misleading. Skill does not make an action ethical or legal. A highly skilled person who enters a system without permission may cause hidden damage, such as deleting small files, installing hidden software, or leaving a path for others to follow later. On the other hand, there is a practice called ethical hacking, where trained experts enter a system with the owner's written permission to find weaknesses and fix them. This is good because the permission and the purpose are clear. The statement would only be true if the word "ethical" were added and permission was clearly given. Therefore, we should say that unauthorised hacking is wrong because it ignores consent and safety, while ethical hacking with permission can be right and helpful.

Q4 (apply): Your classmate finds a website offering a paid educational software for free and asks you to download it together. What would you do and why?
Answer: I would not download the paid software from the free website. That is software piracy, which is the unauthorised copying or use of software without the owner's permission. Even though the website might look harmless, using the software without paying for it means we are taking something that does not belong to us. The people who made the software spent time and money to create it, and they have the right to be paid for their work. If everyone took it for free, the creators would lose money and might stop making useful educational programs. There is also a practical risk in downloading from unknown websites: the file may contain viruses or other harmful programs that could damage the computer or steal personal information. The better and more responsible action is to use free and legal alternatives, such as open-source software from trusted sources, or to ask the teacher or school to buy a licensed copy. In this way, we respect the work of the creators, keep the computer safe, and practise computer ethics.

Q5 (create): Design a five-rule "Digital Citizenship Code" for your school computer lab. Explain how each rule promotes computer ethics and prevents one of the unethical practices.
Answer: Rule 1: Always give credit to the original author when you use information, images, or code from the internet. This promotes honesty and prevents plagiarism. Rule 2: Use only software that the school has installed or that you have a legal licence to use. This supports the creators and prevents software piracy. Rule 3: Never try to log into another student's account or the teacher's computer without permission. This respects privacy and prevents hacking. Rule 4: Think before you post, message, or share anything online. This promotes responsible behaviour and protects others from inappropriate content and privacy risks. Rule 5: Ask for help if you see something unsafe or unethical on the computer. This encourages a culture of responsibility and makes the lab a safe place for learning. Together, these five rules turn the school computer lab into a place where students use the Internet's advantages—information and communication—without falling into its disadvantages.

They must be able to distinguish unauthorised hacking from ethical hacking by explicitly stating that the difference lies in permission, and they must be able to explain why plagiarism is a form of stealing recognition even when no exact words are copied. Finally, the student must be able to apply these principles to a real-life Class 7 scenario, such as deciding whether to download a paid app from a free website, and justify their choice using the vocabulary of credit, licence, and unauthorised access.

title: Digital footprints and safety measures online
definition:
A digital footprint is the persistent trail of data that is left behind by every online activity you perform. Whenever you open a website, search for information, like a post, share a photograph, leave a comment, or watch a video, you add another small piece of information to the record that the internet keeps about you. This record is not stored in one single place; it is spread across many servers, internet service providers, search engines, and social media companies. Even if you later delete a post, the information may already have been copied, screenshotted, shared by someone else, or stored in a backup. That is why experts say that a digital footprint is permanent: every click contributes to a record that is very hard, and sometimes impossible, to erase completely.

Because this trail is so long-lasting, it has real consequences for both online privacy and personal reputation. A digital footprint can reveal what you like, where you go, what you believe, and whom you talk to. Advertisers can use it to show you targeted ads, strangers may use it to guess your habits, and in the worst cases hackers or other unethical users may try to misuse the information. In this node you will study six key safety measures that help you protect your digital identity. A strong password uses a mixture of uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers, and symbols so that it is difficult to guess. Privacy settings are the controls that decide who can see your profile, your posts, and your personal details, a little like curtains on a window. Thinking before posting means pausing to consider whether a comment, photo, or share is safe, respectful, and appropriate, because once it is online it is very hard to take back. Together, these habits help you manage your digital footprint so that it stays a positive record rather than a source of risk.

It is helpful to remember that a digital footprint is not only about social media. Visiting a news website, downloading an application, filling out an online form, or even using a school portal all add to your trail. The vocabulary you need to master includes digital footprint, safety measures, strong password, privacy settings, think before posting, trail, and trace. A strong password is often compared to a strong lock because it takes time and effort to crack. Privacy settings are like the curtains on a window because they let you choose who can look in. Thinking before posting is like thinking before speaking because words that are spoken can be remembered, but words that are posted can be copied and kept forever. By the end of this node you should be able to define a digital footprint, describe at least three safety measures, explain why footprints are permanent, and discuss why they matter for online privacy and reputation.
textWalkthrough:
Let us begin by remembering what you already studied in the previous node, c7_cs_011. There you learnt about computer ethics and unethical practices such as plagiarism, piracy, and hacking. You understood that hacking is an unlawful way of entering someone else's computer system, and that it is closely linked to the misuse of private information. Now, in c7_cs_012, we move from that idea to a more personal question: what kind of information are we ourselves leaving behind every time we use the internet, and how can we protect it? If a hacker tries to misuse data, the data must first exist somewhere. That data exists because our online activities leave trails. So this node explains the digital footprint and the safety measures that keep it from being used against us.

Let us also look back at the depth prerequisite, c6_cs_019. In Class 6 you studied internet safety and online surfing. You learnt how to browse safely, how to judge whether a website is trustworthy, and how to communicate politely and responsibly online. Those lessons were about what you do while you are online. Now, in Class 7, we step back and ask what remains after you have finished browsing. Every safe choice you made in Class 6 is still useful, but now you need to understand the bigger idea: every website visit, every post, and every comment becomes part of a permanent record called a digital footprint. The learning path therefore moves from "how to act safely while online" to "how to manage the lasting identity you are creating through those actions."

The first sub-topic we must understand is the meaning of a digital footprint itself. Imagine that you walk across a long, sandy beach. Each step leaves a mark. Even if the waves wash some of them away, other people may have already noticed where you walked, and the sand still tells a story. The internet is similar. When you visit a website, your browser may store a cookie. When you post a photo, the social media platform saves it. When you share your location with an app, the app records it. All of these marks together form your trail. A good, full answer would say that a digital footprint is the persistent trail of data left by online activities such as browsing, posting, and sharing. A weak answer would say only that it is "something left on the internet." The weak answer is not wrong, but it does not show the examiner that you understand persistence and the variety of activities involved.

Next, let us examine the permanence of digital footprints. This is a common area of confusion, so pay close attention. Suppose you post a comment and then delete it a few minutes later. You may not be able to see it any more, but it may already have been saved in a backup, copied by a friend, or screenshotted by a classmate. Once information is online, it can travel very quickly and very far. Therefore, a strong answer explains that even deleted posts can leave traces, and that every click contributes to a permanent record. A weak answer might say, "I can delete it so it is gone." That answer misses the point and would not earn full marks.

Now we come to the safety measures. There are three main ones in the syllabus. First, use a strong password. A strong password is like a strong lock: it should be a mixture of letters, numbers, and symbols, and it should not be something easy to guess such as your name, your birthday, or the word "password." Second, check the privacy settings on every account you use. Privacy settings are like curtains on windows: they let you control who sees your information. On a social media account, for example, you can decide whether your profile is visible to friends, friends of friends, or the whole world. Third, think before posting. This is like thinking before speaking: once the words are out, you cannot take them back. Before you post a photo, a comment, or a video, ask yourself whether you would be happy for your teacher, your parents, or a future employer to see it.

Finally, why does all this matter? Your digital footprint affects your online privacy and your reputation. Privacy is your right to keep personal information to yourself. If you share too much, strangers can learn about your habits, your home, or your daily routine. Reputation is the opinion other people have of you. A careless post or a shared rumour can stay online for years and affect how teachers, classmates, relatives, or even future employers see you. Examiners expect you to connect these three ideas: digital footprint, safety measures, and their importance for privacy and reputation. A top answer would say, "A digital footprint is permanent because deleted posts can leave traces, so we must use strong passwords, privacy settings, and careful posting to protect our online privacy and reputation."

These marks are called your digital footprint. They can stay there for a long time, even if you try to rub them out. To stay safe, use hard-to-guess passwords, keep your account privacy settings closed to strangers, and think carefully before sharing anything. This helps keep your online life happy and safe.

Answer: This statement is not correct, and there are several reasons to disagree with it. On one side, it is true that many social media platforms and websites allow users to delete their posts, comments, and photographs. This gives us some control over what remains visible on our own profile. Deleting a post can also stop new people from seeing it, which is useful if we have made a small mistake. However, this is only one side of the story. On the other side, once information has been posted online, it can be copied, screenshotted, or shared by others almost instantly. Therefore, even after the original post is deleted, traces of it can remain on other people's devices, on backups, or on other websites. In addition, a deleted post may already have been seen by people, so it can still affect your reputation. Because of this, we should not post anything online thinking that we can simply remove it later. The wiser approach is to think before posting and to keep privacy settings tight. So, while the delete button is helpful, it does not make a post completely disappear. A balanced view is that we should treat every online post as permanent and only share what we are comfortable being seen by many people.

Q4 (apply): You have just created a new social media account. List three safety measures you would take to protect your digital footprint and explain one of them in detail.
Answer: If I created a new social media account, I would take three safety measures. First, I would set a strong password using a mix of uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers, and symbols. Second, I would check the privacy settings and make sure my profile and posts are visible only to people I know and trust. Third, I would think carefully before posting any photo, comment, or personal information. Let me explain the second measure in more detail. Privacy settings are the controls that decide who can see your online activity. Most social media platforms give you options such as "public," "friends only," or "only me." If you choose "friends only," then only the people you have accepted as friends can see your posts. This is like putting curtains on a window: you let in the people you want and keep out strangers. Good privacy settings protect your digital footprint from being seen by people who might misuse your information. They also help you control your online reputation because fewer people can copy or share your content without your knowledge.

Q5 (create): Imagine you are designing a poster for your school about online safety. What three headings would you include, and what advice would you give under each heading?
Answer: If I were designing a poster for my school about online safety, I would use the following three headings: "Lock Your Accounts," "Choose Your Audience," and "Think Before You Post." Under the first heading, "Lock Your Accounts," I would advise students to create strong passwords that mix letters, numbers, and symbols, and to never share those passwords with anyone except a parent or guardian. A strong password is like a strong lock that keeps strangers out. Under the second heading, "Choose Your Audience," I would explain privacy settings and tell students to set their accounts to "friends only" or "private" so that people they do not know cannot see their personal details, photographs, or daily activities. Under the third heading, "Think Before You Post," I would remind students that once something is online, it can be very hard to delete. They should ask themselves if the post is kind, safe, and something they would be happy for teachers or family to see. The poster would include simple pictures, such as a lock, a window with curtains, and a pause button, to make the message clear and memorable.
masteryCriteria: The student must be able to define a digital footprint as a persistent trail of data left by online activities and give at least three concrete examples of activities (browsing, posting, sharing location, downloading, filling forms) that add to it. The student must also be able to describe at least three safety measures — strong passwords, privacy settings, and thinking before posting — and explain in their own words how each one protects online privacy and reputation. Finally, the student must be able to explain why a digital footprint is considered permanent, using the idea that deleted posts can still leave traces on backups, screenshots, and other people's devices, and connect this permanence to the need for careful online behaviour.

title: Cyber ethics capstone - responsible digital citizenship
definition:
Digital citizenship is the responsible and ethical way a person thinks, communicates, and behaves whenever they use computers, the internet, mobile phones, or any digital technology. A responsible digital citizen understands that being online is not a private world without rules; it is a shared public space where every action can affect others. Good digital citizenship is built on three main habits: communicating respectfully, protecting personal information, and respecting the privacy and rights of other people. This means that a student should not send hurtful messages, should not share passwords or personal details, and should not take or spread someone else’s photographs or messages without permission.

One of the most important ideas inside digital citizenship is intellectual property. Intellectual property is the result of human creativity and skill—stories, drawings, photographs, music, films, software, inventions, and designs. Because these creative works take time, effort, and talent, the law protects them. Copyright is the legal protection given to the creator of an original work. In India, the Copyright Act of 1957 (later amended) gives creators the exclusive right to make copies, distribute their work, adapt it, perform it, and display it in public. Copyright applies to books, poems, songs, paintings, photographs, computer programs, and even maps. The creator does not have to register the work for protection; as soon as the work is created in a fixed form, it is protected. This means that an image you find on a search engine, a song on a music app, or a paragraph from an NCERT textbook is usually protected by copyright even if no copyright symbol is shown.

Fair use is a limited exception to copyright that allows people to use small parts of a copyrighted work for specific purposes such as education, research, criticism, news reporting, or comment. In the classroom, fair use lets you quote a few lines from a poem, use a small picture in a project with proper credit, or show a short video clip to explain an idea. However, fair use has boundaries. It does not mean you can copy an entire movie, download a full song, or paste large sections of a website into your own project and call it your own. When fair use is ignored, the result is copyright infringement, which is the use of a copyrighted work without permission or legal excuse. Infringement can also mean plagiarism, which is passing off someone else’s work or ideas as your own without giving credit.

Giving credit means clearly naming the creator, the title of the work, and where it was found. This is not only honest but also shows respect. Responsible digital citizenship, therefore, is the combination of good internet safety and strong ethical behaviour: you keep yourself safe, you keep others safe, and you treat people’s creative work the same way you would want your own work to be treated.
textWalkthrough:
Let us begin by remembering what you already know from earlier in your journey. In Class 5, in node c5_cs_019, you learned about internet safety. You learned that the internet can be a wonderful place, but it also has dangers. You learned how to protect your personal information, how to use strong passwords, and how to be cyber aware—meaning you should notice strange messages, unknown links, and requests from strangers. That was your foundation: keeping yourself safe online. Then, as a direct prerequisite in Class 7, node c7_cs_012 built on that foundation by reminding you that internet safety is not only about technology but also about smart habits. Now, in node c7_cs_025, we take the next step. We move from “How do I stay safe online?” to “How do I behave as a good and responsible member of the online world?” That is exactly what digital citizenship means.

Think of the internet as a large digital neighbourhood. Just as you are expected not to shout rude words in your locality, not to look through your neighbour’s windows, and not to take someone else’s bicycle, the internet also has rules of good behaviour. A good digital citizen is kind and respectful in chat, comment, and email. Suppose a student in a classroom group writes something sarcastic and hurtful about a classmate’s photograph. The bad version of this behaviour is: “It is just a joke; they can take it.” The good version is: “I should check whether my words would hurt the person and whether I have their permission to share that photograph.” Respect is the key word here. Respecting others means treating their feelings, their privacy, and their work as important.

Next, let us think about privacy. Protecting personal information is not only about your passwords and phone number. It is also about other people’s information. For example, if your friend shares a secret with you online, a bad digital citizen might forward it to others, saying, “Everyone will find out anyway.” A good digital citizen keeps the secret and protects their friend’s privacy. The same idea applies to creative work. When someone paints a picture, writes a story, or records a song, that work belongs to them. It is their intellectual property. Copyright is the law that protects this ownership.

Now, how should a student use copyrighted material in school? Imagine you are making a presentation about the Qutub Minar in Delhi. You find a beautiful photograph on the internet. The bad answer would be to copy the whole photograph, put it into your slide, and say nothing about where it came from. The good answer is to use only what is needed, choose a small image, add a caption that says, “Image by [photographer’s name], from [website name or URL],” and explain that the photograph is included for educational use under fair use. Credit is like saying thank you. It tells the creator, “I value your work, and I am not pretending it is mine.”

Let us also compare a strong and a weak explanation. A weak student might write, “Copyright is a rule.” A strong student writes, “Copyright is legal protection given to the creator of an original work such as a book, song, picture, or computer program, and it stops others from copying or using that work without permission.” The difference is that the strong answer gives a clear definition, names examples, and explains the purpose. This is the kind of answer CISCE examiners like to see.

When you sit for your ICSE or ISC board exams in the coming years, examiners will expect you to define concepts clearly, give relevant examples, and show that you can tell the difference between similar ideas. In cyber ethics, a common exam question may ask you to distinguish between fair use and copyright infringement. To answer well, do not just list two words; explain that fair use is limited and educational, while copyright infringement is using a work without permission or proper legal reason. You may also be asked to write short notes on digital citizenship. In such questions, include respectful communication, protection of personal information, respecting privacy, and respecting intellectual property.

Before we close, remember the chain of learning. From c5_cs_019 you learned to guard your own data. From c7_cs_012 you built cyber awareness. In c7_cs_025 you now understand that safety plus respect equals responsible digital citizenship. Whenever you go online, imagine your digital reputation following you like a shadow. Make it a shadow you can be proud of.

If you use a small part of someone else’s work for school, say thank you by giving them credit. This keeps everyone happy and fair.
misconceptionText:
Misconception 1 — “If something is on the internet, it is free and I can use it however I want.”
This is a very common error. CISCE examiners have often noticed that students write definitions or answers that are too vague and do not connect the idea to real examples. A weak answer might say, “Copyright is a rule for books,” without explaining that almost everything online—images, music, videos, and websites—is also protected. The correction is: most creative content on the internet is protected by copyright from the moment it is created. Being online does not remove the owner’s rights. You may use it only with permission, or under a limited exception such as fair use, and you must always give credit.

Misconception 2 — “Fair use means I can copy anything for school.”
This confusion is similar to the examiner observation that some candidates “wrote the direct answer without showing the working or steps.” In cyber ethics, students sometimes jump to the conclusion that any school use is fair use. The correction is: fair use is limited. It allows only small portions for specific educational purposes. Copying an entire movie, song, image collection, or article is not fair use. It becomes copyright infringement. A good answer explains both the purpose (education) and the limitation (small portion, with credit).

Misconception 3 — “Plagiarism and copyright infringement are the same thing, so if I give credit I can copy anything.”
This is another frequent mistake. Students sometimes confuse two related ideas and end up giving only one definition or only examples, without showing both. The correction is: plagiarism is an academic and ethical problem—using someone else’s work or ideas as your own without credit. Copyright infringement is a legal problem—using a protected work without permission or a valid legal reason. Giving credit helps you avoid plagiarism, but it does not by itself solve copyright problems. You still need permission or fair use. A complete answer should define both terms separately and give an example of each.
diagnosticText:
Q1 (recall): Define digital citizenship, copyright, and fair use in your own words.
Answer: Digital citizenship is the responsible and ethical behaviour of a person who uses digital technology and the internet. It includes communicating respectfully with others, protecting personal information, respecting the privacy of other people, and following the rules that keep online spaces safe and fair. Copyright is the legal right that protects an original creative work from being copied, used, or distributed without the creator’s permission. This protection applies to books, poems, songs, pictures, photographs, films, and computer programs. In India, the Copyright Act of 1957 provides this protection, and the owner has the exclusive right to reproduce, publish, perform, and adapt the work. Fair use is a limited exception that allows someone to use a small part of a copyrighted work for purposes such as education, research, news reporting, criticism, or comment. For example, a student may quote a few lines from a poem or use a small image in a school project with proper credit. However, fair use does not allow copying the whole work or using it for commercial profit.

Q2 (reasoning): Why is it important to respect copyright when using pictures, music, or text you find online?
Answer: Respecting copyright is important because creative work takes time, skill, and effort to produce. When a photographer takes a picture, a musician records a song, or an author writes an article, they are creating something of value. Copyright gives them the legal right to control how that work is used and to receive recognition or payment for it. If we copy their work without permission or credit, we take away their right to benefit from their own creation. This is unfair to the creator and can also be illegal. Respecting copyright also encourages people to keep creating new and useful content for everyone. In a school setting, respecting copyright means using only small parts of works, choosing material carefully, and giving clear credit. It also helps students learn honesty and responsibility, which are important qualities of a good digital citizen.

Q3 (evaluate): A student says, “I found an image on Google, so I can use it in my school project without asking because it is educational.” Evaluate this statement.
Answer: This statement is partly true but mostly incorrect, and it shows a misunderstanding of how copyright and fair use work. It is true that education is one of the purposes for which fair use may apply. A student may be allowed to use a small part of a copyrighted image in a school project if the use is limited, non-commercial, and properly credited. However, simply finding an image on a search engine does not mean it is free to use. Most images on Google are protected by copyright, and the owner’s rights still exist whether or not the image has a copyright symbol. Using the full image without permission, downloading it, and placing it in a project without giving credit would usually be considered copyright infringement, not fair use. The student also confuses the idea of educational purpose with unlimited permission. Fair use is not a free pass; it is a narrow exception with conditions. A correct approach would be to use a small portion of the image, or an image with a Creative Commons or public-domain licence, and always provide credit. Therefore, the statement is not fully correct because it ignores both the need for credit and the limits of fair use.

Q4 (apply): Your teacher asks you to prepare a short digital poster about famous Indian monuments. You find a photograph of the Taj Mahal and a paragraph from a travel website. Describe the correct steps you would take to use these materials ethically.
Answer: First, I would decide what I really need from the photograph and the paragraph. For the photograph, I should not copy the full high-resolution image if a smaller version is enough. I would check the website for a copyright or licence statement. If the image is marked as free for educational use or Creative Commons, I would still give full credit. For the Taj Mahal image, I would write the caption like this: “Photograph of the Taj Mahal, by [name if known], from [website name], used for educational purpose under fair use.” For the paragraph from the travel website, I would not copy it word-for-word. Instead, I would read the information, close the website, and write the facts in my own words. If I want to use a short quotation, I would keep it brief, place it inside quotation marks, and mention the source. This way I avoid plagiarism and copyright infringement. I would also make a list of all sources at the bottom of my poster. These steps show that I am a responsible digital citizen who respects both copyright and the hard work of creators.

Q5 (create): Design a “Digital Citizen Pledge” that a Class 7 student could sign and follow for one week. Include at least four promises that show responsible and ethical online behaviour.
Answer: My Digital Citizen Pledge: “This week, I promise to be a responsible and respectful digital citizen. First, I will think before I post, comment, or share, making sure my words are kind and helpful, not hurtful. Second, I will protect my own privacy and the privacy of others by not sharing personal information, passwords, photographs, or messages without permission. Third, I will respect copyright and intellectual property by giving credit to creators and using only small parts of online content for schoolwork under fair use. Fourth, I will not copy and paste others’ work and claim it as my own; instead, I will write in my own words and list my sources. Fifth, I will ask a teacher or parent if I am unsure whether something is safe or fair to use. By following these promises, I will show that I am a responsible digital citizen who helps make the internet a better place for everyone.”
masteryCriteria: To master this node, the student must be able to clearly define digital citizenship, copyright, and fair use in their own words and distinguish fair use from copyright infringement and from plagiarism using at least one concrete example for each. The student must also be able to evaluate a real online situation (such as copying an image found on a search engine for a school project) and correctly judge whether it is fair use, infringement, or plagiarism, giving reasons that reference the size of the portion used, the purpose, and whether credit was given. Finally, the student must be able to apply these ideas by listing the correct ethical steps for using a photograph and a paragraph from a website in a school poster, and by creating a personal Digital Citizen Pledge that includes respectful communication, privacy protection, and respect for intellectual property.
